Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. And that’s it.
“They don’t record,” Himel says. “The only thing they do, which is the same thing as an Alexa device in your house or some other devices, they’re just listening for a specific wake word. They’re not sending anything … If they hear [the wake word], then they start listening to what you’re saying. When you’re done talking, then it’s processing, and that’s visible to the AI. It gets processed, and that’s kind of it.”
Slipping them on, they’re comfortable and, I think, quite fetching on me. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.
Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3
I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. I’m told I can pull it off, but I keep asking my colleague Jay Peters if I’m giving ’80s serial killer vibes. The other new style is called Zena — not the warrior princess — and it’s a bolder, geometric cat-eye frame.
The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. There’s a sixth microphone, compared to the second generation’s five, for clearer phone calls. Battery life has gotten a slight boost to nine hours, an hour longer than the second gen. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. Sure! That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options.
Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They start at $449, up from $379 for the second-gen models last year.
Meta Glasses — the off-brand, more affordable entry-level glasses launched a few months ago — also have more options. There are two new styles, Capri and Nova. Capri is some kind of cat-eye shape, while Nova… honestly, the styles are all starting to blur together. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. There’s a new ivory-colored Kylie Jenner pair that costs $399.
But maybe Kylie Jenner isn’t the celebrity collab you’ve been dreaming about. That’s fine. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. They have pink lenses and come with a blind-box-type charm styled after Lisa’s pets. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.)
Why the celebrity collabs? Options for more people, including women.
“With the Meta Glasses Starfire with Kylie, we saw a younger, more female audience start to buy the glasses,” says Himel. “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.”
There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. I suspect I’d need to make a spreadsheet to list them all. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. That, I suspect, is the...

title_en: Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 hands-on: Better battery life and a price hike
title_fa: Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 hands-on: Better battery life and a price hike
excerpt_en: The latest lineup comes in two new frame styles: Aviator and Zena.
excerpt_fa: The latest lineup comes in two new frame styles: Aviator and Zena.
content_en:
Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 hands-on: Better battery life and a price hike
The latest lineup comes in two new frame styles: Aviator and Zena.
Meta just showed off its third-generation lineup of Ray-Ban-branded AI glasses, and the latest frames come with more hours of battery life and a bit of a price hike. Starting at $449, the Gen 3 Ray-Ban Meta Glasses now come in an Aviator style and a more angular frame called Zena.
Some of the most noticeable changes will look familiar if you've used the Ray-Ban Meta Optics line or any of the Meta Glasses line. Like those, the Gen 3 frames also come with a programmable action button. This can be customized to trigger a specific Meta AI command, capture mode or just about any other feature. The glasses also come with the same adjustable temple tips that we saw on the Optics line, which should make for a slightly better fit.
Speaking of fit, the aviator frames are quite a bit thicker than some other Ray-Ban Meta models I've tried, and they did feel a bit loose on my face. It's a bolder style than the boxy Wayfarers we're used to seeing from Meta (there is a Gen 3 Wayfarer model too) but I was just happy to see another tortoiseshell frame. As always, what looks lame on one person's face might look cool on someone else.
The most important Gen 3 upgrades aren't immediately visible: better battery life and microphones. According to Meta, the Gen 3 line now top out at 9 hours of battery life. I haven't had my pair long enough to test this out but in my experience, battery life claims really depend on how close your use is to what Meta considers "typical." For example, I got a little more than 5 hours from my Gen 2 Ray-Ban Meta glasses with continuous audio playback. Either way, another hour should be noticeable enough for anyone wearing these for extended sessions.
Meta has also added an extra mic to its Gen 3 frames, bringing the total number of microphones to six. The company says this should reduce background noise to make it easier for people (or its AI) to hear you in noisy environments.
Some of the updates I'm most looking forward to trying aren't out yet. These include the ability to — finally — capture photos and videos in landscape orientation. (This capability will eventually roll out to other models too.) The Gen 3 line will also be the first to support recording with Dolby Atmos in videos, and allow users to capture spatial sound alongside their videos. I feel like this is a somewhat niche feature, but I'm interested to see how much of a difference it makes.
One of the biggest benefits of Gen 3 is just how many options Meta now offers. "Meta Glasses" used to be synonymous with dark Wayfarers, but that's no longer the case. Between Ray-Ban, Oakley and its own Meta-branded line, the company says that it will have more than 100 different frame styles and color variations by the end of the year.

title_en: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
title_fa: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
excerpt_en: Nothing says Italian craftsmanship like a Chinese robot doing a lasso to "L'Amour Toujours."
excerpt_fa: Nothing says Italian craftsmanship like a Chinese robot doing a lasso to "L'Amour Toujours."
content_en:
Vogue World closed its Milan edition this week with a troupe of robots — perhaps a preview of what’s coming when the event descends on San Francisco next year.
Vogue World is the magazine’s annual traveling spectacle, now in its fifth year: part runway show, part celebrity showcase, part variety hour, part ad-sales opportunity, staged in a different city each time. It has run through New York, London, Paris, and Hollywood. This year’s Milan edition was marketed as a tribute to Italian craftsmanship and “the human touch” in an age of technology, which makes what happened next a little strange.
During the act titled The Age of Intelligence, humanoid robots made by the Chinese firm Unitree walked into the Galleria to Gigi D’Agostino’s “L’Amour Toujours.” They waved their arms in the air, imploring onlookers to clap. One did a lasso. They were not wearing clothes. The pained expression of Alessandro Michele, the creative director of Valentino, quickly went viral.
I haven’t seen a single thing about the actual fashion that was presented at Vogue World Milan. Instead, everyone is talking about the robots. (These same robots have been making headlines worldwide for their dance moves, and for falling and breaking.) Similar robots turned up on the runway at London Fashion Week, which is happening now.
Vogue turned heads earlier this year when it announced that the next edition will be in San Francisco, arguably one of the least stylish cities in the United States. The timing isn’t coincidental. Anna Wintour has aligned herself ever more closely with the tech barons of our time, and Vogue World Milan was itself sponsored in part by Meta Glasses, with additional support from OpenAI.
It was one of those moments that reveals how thoroughly tech exists in a bubble, and that not everyone is happy with the rapid adoption of new technology, or by Vogue cozying up to the symbols of the insanely rich — and only getting richer — tech titans during a cost-of-living crisis. That’s before you get to AI, mass surveillance, the displacement of labor, and the energy crisis, all of them overseen by the same titans. For some, a robot on a runway is further proof of what is going wrong in the world right now.
“I’m annoyed by the celebrities cheering the whole thing,” one tech founder wrote me on Instagram. “It’s sick and gloom. People are literally losing jobs and livelihoods because of these things. They need to stop encouraging it. What’s it even modeling? Headphones?”
One fashion reporter friend simply said “No,” when I asked for thoughts on the robots and Vogue World San Francisco. Jason Johnson, founder of Culture Impact Agency, noted that Vogue has been trying to build a relationship with Silicon Valley for at least the past decade, highlighting when Jony Ive co-hosted the Met Gala back in 2015. The dancing robots at Vogue World Milan were inevitable, then, as is Vogue World San Francisco and as was Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, getting the splashy Vogue wedding cover and co-hosting the 2026 Met Gala.
“Publications are figuring out new ways to make money and tech has money,” he told me. “Vogue has the cultural influence and access that those tech people want.” Both sides win in the end, he said.
Still, something about the way Vogue is going about this feels unnatural.
Muna Ikedionwu, founder of MKEDI, a strategy firm for early-stage startups, said what she found most interesting about the robots is that they don’t fully represent the innovation and progress that’s actually happening in the creative technologist space. “I’ve seen such incredible examples of engineering and AI being used to influence fashion, being used to influence design and art,” she told me, adding that robots walking down the runway doesn’t even scratch the surface of what is happening right now at the intersection of fashion and tech.
She points to the artist duo AA Murakami, who created Olympian Eileen Gu’s dress of bubbles at this year’s Met Gala. They are fashion designers but also engineers, Ikedionwu said, noting a presentation she saw them give recently about how to create an “everlasting bubble.” They are helping to pioneer “emphemeral technology,” she said, “this idea of technology and innovation that speaks to the ephemeral nature or the temporariness of art and humanity and the soul.”
Sure, I guess when you compare it to this, the robots did seem quite boring. Whenever I think about the intersection of fashion and technology, I think about that Spring 2024 Schiaparelli collection, which unveiled a robot baby crafted with Swarovski crystals and a dress made with vintage tech like PC microchips. (I once threatened to wear that dress to Disrupt; see image above.)
Ikedionwu wonders whether this robot performance was a way to make the general public more comfortable with technology and fashion overlapping, a merger that has been underway behind the scenes for years. If so, it didn’t work. But maybe Vogue World is saving all the good stuff for San Francisco.

title_en: Meta announces Ray-Ban Meta Audio, its first smart glasses without a camera
title_fa: Meta announces Ray-Ban Meta Audio, its first smart glasses without a camera
excerpt_en: That's one way to avoid the whole surreptitious recording issues.
excerpt_fa: That's one way to avoid the whole surreptitious recording issues.
content_en:
Meta announces Ray-Ban Meta Audio, its first smart glasses without a camera
A $349 alternative to "pervert glasses."
Invasive use of Meta's camera-enabled smart glasses has earned them the moniker "pervert glasses," and the company has prepped a solution for Meta Connect 2026: Ray-Ban Meta Audio, smart glasses that ditch cameras entirely to focus on audio features and AI.
Naturally, Meta doesn't characterize the new glasses as a response to public backlash — though they are making it harder to use the camera-equipped kind for surreptitious filming — but rather as an acknowledgement that audio has always been its smart glasses' most popular feature. The new frames are capable of taking calls, letting you respond to messages with your voice and playing back podcasts and music without cutting you off from the rest of the world. They're also a way to access Meta AI for things like live translation and real-time answers to questions.
Another way of looking at the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is as a way to get many of the hardware improvements of the company's latest models, without the extra baggage. Meta says they'll last up to 12 hours on a single charge, with an additional 48 hours available if you use their charging case. They also include the same fit adjustments as the company's previous frames, with the option for adjustable temple tips, customizable nose pads and overextension hinges (hinges with springs that can accommodate a wider selection of head shapes and widths) for improved comfort. Ditching the cameras also means the glasses are lighter at 43 grams; Meta's other models weigh anywhere from 49.2 grams (the recent Optics glasses) to 69 grams (the largest size of Meta Ray-Ban Display).
The real win for Meta and anyone potentially curious about the company's smart glasses is that removing the camera and recording light makes these new frames look even more normal than before. Unless you clocked the slightly larger temples and cut-outs for speakers, you might not know the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are anything other than Ray-Bans. The company is selling the new glasses in two new styles, a rectangular option called Burbank and a retro-inspired style called Clubmaster, both in 23 colors and lens combinations. They also support a range of optical prescriptions, according to the company.
At this moment in Meta's public perception, releasing the Ray-Ban Meta Audio isn't likely to convert critics, but they could convince someone uncomfortable with the optics of smart glasses in general. Unless of course Meta does something to make people even more mad, like actually releasing the facial recognition feature it was previously testing.
The Ray-Ban Meta Audio ship October 13 and are available to pre-order today starting at $349.

title_en: Meta brings FDA-cleared hearing enhancement to its smart glasses
title_fa: Meta brings FDA-cleared hearing enhancement to its smart glasses
excerpt_en: After a free trial it'll cost $150 to add on, or require a Meta One subscription.
excerpt_fa: After a free trial it'll cost $150 to add on, or require a Meta One subscription.
content_en:
Meta brings FDA-cleared hearing enhancement to its smart glasses
But it'll cost you extra.
Meta's AI Glasses are getting a new feature made for wearers with hearing loss. During Meta Connect, the company announced that it's rolling out Hearing Enhancement to supported Meta Glasses later this year (that doesn't include the Ray-Ban models, at least to start). Users can access it as part of a Meta One subscription, or pay a one-time cost of $149. There's also the option to try a 30-day free trial before committing.
The software has been cleared by the FDA and is eligible for HSA/FSA reimbursement, though you'd have to sort that out with your insurance carrier. It doesn't require a prescription and users can set it up at home. Wearers will be able to activate it or turn it off any time with a voice command ("Hey Meta, start Hearing Enhancement").
While Meta already offers a Conversation Focus mode to improve audibility in noisy environments, this new feature is designed specifically for users with mild to moderate hearing loss who may normally use a hearing aid. It comes alongside improvements to Meta Glasses' Detailed Responses feature based on feedback from the blind and low-vision community, as well as new customizable audio and controls.

title_en: Meta's Muse AI agent is coming to its AI glasses
title_fa: Meta's Muse AI agent is coming to its AI glasses
excerpt_en: Have your virtual assistant book a flight while you're jogging.
excerpt_fa: Have your virtual assistant book a flight while you're jogging.
content_en:
Meta's Muse AI agent is coming to its AI glasses
Have your virtual assistant book a flight while you’re jogging.
Meta's Muse AI agent can do a lot. If you're willing to trust it with the most sensitive parts of your digital life, it can use the web, book travel, make phone calls, send emails and even make purchases on your behalf. So far, you can use Muse in its standalone iOS, Android or Mac apps, or within your WhatsApp chats. But in "the coming months," Meta is bringing its errand-running agent to its AI glasses.
Meta shared more details about Muse for AI glasses at its Connect 2026 event on Wednesday. The company said Muse will help you "stay on top of things, take tasks and projects off your plate and turn long-term goals into action plans, all hands-free." Specific examples include booking appointments, checking flight prices and tracking down items.
Muse, which launched earlier this month, asks for permission before carrying out tasks that involve sensitive actions like making purchases. You can choose which outside services it can access and revoke those connections at any time.
Once Muse for glasses launches, you'll be able to activate it by saying its name and making a request. It will work in the background and check in with you when it's finished.
But that gets to a question about how much Muse for glasses really adds: agentic AI's appeal is that it does things in the background without constant supervision. Pulling out your phone to give it a new task doesn't exactly sound like much of a burden. The glasses do make that hands-free, and Meta suggested some situations where that could be useful: guiding personalized workouts, logging meals and providing nutritional insights. But that sounds like more of a convenience than a necessity. Still, if you're investing in the privacy-threatening "perv glasses" anyway, you may as well get Meta's new personal AI agent to go with them, right?

content_en:
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
Muse started as a chatbot but will soon be an AI avatar you can talk with over video.
Muse started as a chatbot but will soon be an AI avatar you can talk with over video.

title_en: The purpose of the triangle symbol on your Samsung Galaxy phone
title_fa: The purpose of the triangle symbol on your Samsung Galaxy phone
excerpt_en: Samsung phones have a few different triangle symbols that can display in the status bar in different scenarios. This is how to tell what they mean.
excerpt_fa: Samsung phones have a few different triangle symbols that can display in the status bar in different scenarios. This is how to tell what they mean.
content_en:
The purpose of the triangle symbol on your Samsung Galaxy phone
Turns out, it could mean a variety of things.
Your Samsung Galaxy smartphone is feature-packed with numerous on-screen icons to show you what's going on. One shows a broken triangle symbol that depicts two arrows pointing up and down. If you spot it, it's nothing sinister. It means Data Saver is active on your device, protecting your data allowance. So, what is Data Saver? What does it do, and how do you switch it off?
Data Saver is usually one of three triangle-shaped indicators:
- Data Saver, depicted by a broken triangle on a light background featuring two small arrows pointing up and down.
- A solid dark triangle with a centrally placed exclamation mark is an error warning. This may reflect a charging fault or a software glitch.
- A plain triangle means cellular roaming is active.
To add a little confusion, some icons can vary by phone model and carrier, but the above are the median meanings.
Is Data Saver good or bad?
Many Galaxy users may never come across Data Saver, as it is usually off by default. The controls are situated in Settings > Connections > Data usage, where you toggle it on or off.
Samsung's Data Saver mode is neither good nor bad. It exists to help manage mobile data use. When active, apps cannot access the internet in the background — only your currently active app can do so, and as soon as you open another app, its connection stops. This also means background app processes such as uploading video will not take place. While not its primary purpose, Data Saver also nurses battery life by preventing background connections.
Data Saver isn't going to do much for you if you spend most of your time on a Wi-Fi network, as you have all the data you need. It comes into its own when your allocated monthly bandwidth runs low or when you are traveling. It is important to recognize that there are trade-offs to its use, as when in that mode, your background apps cannot do any of the following:
- Download updates
- Sync data
- Fetch new content
- Receive alerts and notifications
You can let some apps work normally
To overcome these limitations, you can give specific apps permission to continue working in the background while Data Saver is on.
- Open Settings > Connections > Data usage.
- Tap Allowed to use data while Data Saver is on.
Menu wording can differ depending on model and software version
In the next dialog, choose which apps you want to permit; typically these will be your communication apps, but you can assign this permission to any listed app.
Do I turn Data Saver on or off?
If you are mostly on Wi-Fi, you probably won't need Data Saver. However, if you are traveling and want to manage sometimes expensive roaming charges, you may need to turn it on.

title_en: Meta Connect 2026: The biggest news and announcements
title_fa: Meta Connect 2026: The biggest news and announcements
excerpt_en: It’s about time for Meta Connect, the company’s annual product launch event. This year, given the company’s major focus on AI and wearables like smart glasses, it seems likely that we’ll see updates from CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team on those categories. The company has been...

content_en:
It’s about time for Meta Connect, the company’s annual product launch event. This year, given the company’s major focus on AI and wearables like smart glasses, it seems likely that we’ll see updates from CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team on those categories. The company has been facing significant scrutiny because of how some users have been covertly recording other people using the glasses, meaning that one of the biggest announcements of the show could be its rumored camera-free pair.
Connect has also traditionally been a venue for updates on Meta’s VR hardware and software. While the company has scaled back its VR ambitions, a recent leak seemingly revealing some kind of unannounced mixed reality glasses could indicate that Meta will show off new immersive headwear technology during the event.
Zuckerberg’s keynote is scheduled to begin at 7PM ET / 4PM PT on Wednesday, September 23rd. Follow along with all of our coverage right here.
Meta is making a standalone Muse AI gadget
Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent. The product, called Muse Charm, was briefly shown off by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at the end of tonight’s Meta Connect presentation. It looks almost like a chunky smartwatch without the strap — just a big screen, plus a little lanyard for carrying the device around.
The Muse Charm has a fingerprint sensor on the top right corner that you can press to activate and begin speaking to the agent. There appears to be a small camera on the device as well, plus what looks like at least three holes for microphones on the front. Zuckerberg said you don’t have to unlock a phone or open an app to use the Charm, but he didn’t share how it’s actually connecting to Meta’s servers.
Read Article >Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.
You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.
Read Article >- Soon, you’ll be able to rent or buy movies right on your Quest headset.
Meta is promising that “hundreds” of movies will be available “later this year” in the US, with “thousands of titles available internationally” when the new Meta VR Glasses launch in spring 2027.
Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket.
The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. It felt like a lightweight Vision Pro, and is perhaps a better execution of some of what Apple wanted to do with that device.
Read Article >Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it’s “working on” bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they’re looking at.
Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta’s glasses. They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses. Meta AI will also be able to give “more context-rich answers” when users ask the glasses what they’re looking at, potentially making Meta’s glasses more effective for helping blind and low-vision users interpret their surroundings. A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side.
Read Article >Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern.
Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.

How will Meta address privacy concerns around its glasses?

title_en: Anthropic says its biology lab has already found something big
title_fa: Anthropic says its biology lab has already found something big
excerpt_en: But maybe the biggest reveal is that Anthropic has not let Claude run loose in its biology lab. Humans are still, so far, in the loop.
excerpt_fa: But maybe the biggest reveal is that Anthropic has not let Claude run loose in its biology lab. Humans are still, so far, in the loop.
content_en:
Last week, Anthropic confirmed that it was operating a wet biology lab in the Bay Area where it uses its AI models to run physical experiments. This week, the AI giant announced that this lab has already made what it believes is a big discovery: a new enzyme “system” that has certain “properties reminiscent of CRISPR,” as Anthropic describes it.
CRISPR is a natural immune system used by bacteria to fight off viruses that has become a gene-editing technology widely used by researchers.
Essentially, what Anthropic says it found is a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect and replicate within bacteria. Anthropic’s researchers say this system behaves similarly to CRISPR in that it can “perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA.”
It will be up to the broader research community to validate how big, or new, this discovery actually is. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei acknowledges that the discovery was based on the work of others and that a team from Stanford previously discovered a system “that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found,” he wrote on X.
But Amodei and Anthropic are not just emphasizing the discovery. They are touting it was found “mostly, though not entirely, by Claude,” the CEO wrote.
On the one hand, that is astounding. This lab was only established this spring (though Anthropic declined to be more specific about how many months it has been open). A discovery in just a few short months would be speedy enough work, but the team said it actually only took Claude 21 hours of concerted effort. Claude searched through data using about 950 agents that burned through 210 million tokens.
Still, the revelation that Anthropic has been conducting biology experiments comes right after AI CEOs, including Amodei, publicly admitted that models have become so capable, and so potentially dangerous, that the industry must slow down and develop safety-testing procedures. This after a couple of his employees publicly said earlier this month that there’s a risk AI could kill us all.
Amodei himself has said one of the things he fears most is that AI could be used for bioterrorism. But he also believes AI will “cure most diseases in 5-10 years,” he wrote. So Anthropic has clearly decided the rewards are worth the risks.
Given that, perhaps the biggest reveal in this news isn’t the discovery itself but that the biology lab hasn’t let Claude loose. The physical experiments were done by humans.
“Our lab, located in the Bay Area, looks like a typical molecular biology lab. We do research that involves only the lower-levels of the biosafety risk level (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and we do not handle pathogens that can infect humans. All of the lab work is performed by human scientists.”
It’s also true that AI-powered biological research is hardly unique to Anthropic. Researchers from Stanford just published a paper on the work they are doing with LLMs and CRISPR. Researchers at UC San Francisco used AI to design enzymes from scratch. Google launched its first AI-powered biology research tool, AlphaFold, back in 2020. So AI has clearly arrived in biological research beyond the AI labs pursuing it themselves.
Yet, Amodei hasn’t ruled out a fully automated biology lab in the future. “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today,” he said.
.

title_en: If Amazon doesn’t know how to eliminate carbon emissions, then who does?
title_fa: If Amazon doesn’t know how to eliminate carbon emissions, then who does?
excerpt_en: Amazon is one of the largest companies in the world. How much responsibility does it have to meet its net-zero pledge?
excerpt_fa: Amazon is one of the largest companies in the world. How much responsibility does it have to meet its net-zero pledge?
content_en:
Amazon’s chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company doesn’t know how it will achieve its goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2040.
“We are still striving towards that target,” Kara Hurst said at an Axios event, adding later that she is “not going to sit here and say, ‘We know all the ways that we’re going to do this.’”
The admission was both frank and realistic. It’s also a bit disappointing. If Amazon doesn’t have a plan to decarbonize, then who does?
Amazon is one of the largest companies in the world, with last year’s revenue up 12% to $717 billion — about the size of Ireland’s economy. Its rise is illustrative of how, as UN Secretary General António Guterres has pointed out, power has shifted from governments to a few corporations.
As power moves, responsibility follows. The question is, how much responsibility does Amazon bear?
“This isn’t a question of companies versus governments,” Hurst told TechCrunch in a written reply to questions after the event. “Tackling climate change at the scale it demands takes both, and it takes them working together.” She added, “Where we can lead, we do.”
It’s true that Amazon has not been sitting still. In her talk yesterday, Hurst pointed out that the company is “one of the largest purchasers of clean energy in the world for the last several years running” with 42 gigawatts in its portfolio. She also said that Amazon has reduced its carbon intensity, or how much pollution it generates per dollar of revenue, though that claim depends on the time frame. Last year, carbon intensity rose compared with 2024, even though it stayed below where it was in 2022.
Amazon is a sprawling business, and as a result, its carbon emissions are spread across nearly every sector of the economy, from aviation and AI to agriculture and construction. The company needs suppliers in every sector to achieve its goal. “This is not something we can do alone,” Hurst said at the Axios event.
The company acknowledges that its commitments are its own. “We hold ourselves accountable to The Climate Pledge goal of net-zero carbon by 2040. That commitment hasn’t changed,” Hurst told TechCrunch.
But Amazon has also made choices that undermine its leadership on the issue. Earlier this year, an investigation revealed the company’s plans to build a 7.65 gigawatt natural gas power plant to power an AI data center campus. The project’s 35 turbines could release up to 33 million tons of carbon dioxide annually, making it the largest single source of that pollution in the U.S.
With few exceptions, companies prioritize revenue growth over climate commitments. For a company like Amazon, which operates the largest cloud service in the world, AI is apparently a revenue driver that’s impossible to pass up.

Amazon’s chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company doesn’t know how it will achieve its goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2040.
“We are still striving towards that target,” Kara Hurst said at an Axios event, adding later that she is “not going to sit here and say, ‘We know all the ways that we’re going to do this.’”
The admission was both frank and realistic. It’s also a bit disappointing. If Amazon doesn’t have a plan to decarbonize, then who does?
Amazon is one of the largest companies in the world, with last year’s revenue up 12% to $717 billion — about the size of Ireland’s economy. Its rise is illustrative of how, as UN Secretary General António Guterres has pointed out, power has shifted from governments to a few corporations.
As power moves, responsibility follows. The question is, how much responsibility does Amazon bear?
“This isn’t a question of companies versus governments,” Hurst told TechCrunch in a written reply to questions after the event. “Tackling climate change at the scale it demands takes both, and it takes them working together.” She added, “Where we can lead, we do.”

Last year, carbon intensity rose compared with 2024, even though it stayed below where it was in 2022.
Amazon is a sprawling business, and as a result, its carbon emissions are spread across nearly every sector of the economy, from aviation and AI to agriculture and construction. The company needs suppliers in every sector to achieve its goal. “This is not something we can do alone,” Hurst said at the Axios event.

Earlier this year, an investigation revealed the company’s plans to build a 7.65 gigawatt natural gas power plant to power an AI data center campus. The project’s 35 turbines could release up to 33 million tons of carbon dioxide annually, making it the largest single source of that pollution in the U.S.

title_en: ShinyHunters hackers claim to have 2-3TB of sensitive information about FBI employees
title_fa: ShinyHunters hackers claim to have 2-3TB of sensitive information about FBI employees
excerpt_en: Financial extortion doesn't seem to be the group's goal this time.
excerpt_fa: Financial extortion doesn't seem to be the group's goal this time.
content_en:
ShinyHunters hackers claim to have 2-3TB of sensitive information about FBI employees
Financial extortion doesn’t seem to be the group’s goal this time.
Hacking group ShinyHunters has allegedly stolen extensive amounts of sensitive information from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation that includes details about its employees and job applicants. Reuters reports that it has seen a sample of the data obtained by the attack on the agency, and 404 Media also said it received confirmation of the action from a representative of ShinyHunters. The hackers also appeared responsible for an unauthorized takeover of the FBI website earlier this week.
"We hacked the FBI. We hold data on all FBI employees and applicants," the spokesperson told 404 Media. According to that source, ShinyHunters got the information by using a zero day exploit in the PeopleSoft program from Oracle to obtain access to Amazon Web Services' GovCloud servers.
A statement from the FBI shared with Reuters said that the agency was aware of "a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information" and that it is "actively and aggressively investigating the matter."
The attackers claim to have 2-3TB of data, but the sample shared with the media appeared to contain names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for 5,000 employees at the FBI. The group may also have gathered details about some work assignments for agents and about some FBI units that are working on intelligence, security and counter-espionage efforts, including operations focused on both China and Russia.
Many of ShinyHunters' previous hacks have been aimed at extortion, with actions against parties ranging from Ticketmaster to Rockstar Games in recent years. However, the rep who spoke with 404 Media claimed this move against the FBI was "not financially motivated" but rather aimed at coercing the government agency to remove or amend a previous statement made about ShinyHunters. In a report from May, the FBI said the hacking group "exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims."

title_en: VC firm Bessemer now has another $5.75B to invest in (what else?) AI
title_fa: VC firm Bessemer now has another $5.75B to invest in (what else?) AI
excerpt_en: The VC firm says that AI-native companies are growing faster than any technology, ever.
excerpt_fa: The VC firm says that AI-native companies are growing faster than any technology, ever.
content_en:
Bessemer Venture Partners announced on Wednesday that it has raised $5.75 billion across two new funds to accelerate its investment across all parts of the AI stack. The firm, which has backed companies such as Anthropic, Cognition, Legora, Perplexity, Ramp, Shopify, and Waymo, dedicated $1.75 billion for seed and early-stage investing and the remaining $4 billion for growth startups.
Bessemer has been well-known as a leading VC in the SaaS era, with a particular knack for picking enterprise winners, like Box, Docusign, and Gainsight. Since 2022, it has invested in more than 260 AI-native companies. So far, the firm has invested $3 billion into AI-related startups, it says, including those focused on compute, infrastructure, foundation models, dev tools, app-layer startups, and agentic tech.
Now, Bessemer positions all things AI as the opportunity of a lifetime — a common sentiment, until the next big trendy tech revolution comes around, of course.
“AI-native companies are scaling faster than any category of technology we’ve backed before,” Bessemer Partner Byron Deeter said in the company’s funding announcement. VC firms also need to keep increasing their war chests, Deeter told Bloomberg, because companies staying private longer has become “a permanent structural shift.”

title_en: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
title_fa: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
excerpt_en: Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm's latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price...
excerpt_fa: Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm's latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price...
content_en:
Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price tags (thanks RAMageddon!).
Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
The Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch both have better battery life and performance, but higher price tags.
The Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch both have better battery life and performance, but higher price tags.
While the 12-inch Surface Pro started at $799.99 last year, it’s debuting on October 13th at a starting price of $1,149.99. Likewise, the 13-inch Surface Laptop was originally priced at $899.99, but it’s up to $1,199.99 this time around. There’s no base 8GB model this time, causing some of the price increase, as both devices launch with a minimum of 16GB of RAM and can be configured up to 24GB.
Pricing aside, Microsoft is promising that the six-core Snapdragon X2 Plus chips will deliver up to 18 percent more efficient battery performance, more than 60 percent faster graphics performance, and up to 95 percent faster local AI inferencing on the built-in NPU.
That’s a lot of percentages, but what it equates to on these devices is better battery life and improved performance. On the Surface Pro 12-inch Second Edition, as Microsoft calls it, that means an extra hour of web browsing (up to 13 hours in total), and on the Surface Laptop 13-inch Second Edition it’s two extra hours of web browsing usage (up to 18 hours in total).
Microsoft is using similar displays on these models as last year, so the Surface Pro 12-inch has a 2196 x 1464 (220 PPI) LCD display that runs at up to 90Hz. The Surface Laptop 13-inch still ships with a 1920 x 1280 (178 PPI) display that only runs at 60Hz. Both displays have been upgraded from 400 nits of brightness to 500 nits, though.
Port selection remains the same, too. Both devices include two USB-C 3.2 ports, and the Surface Laptop 13-inch also has a USB-A 3.2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Both also support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity.
I’m surprised that Microsoft hasn’t upgraded at least one of these smaller Surface devices with a haptic trackpad, particularly because Windows 11 now adds subtle haptic nudges, and the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with haptic feedback. Microsoft is launching a second edition of its Surface Mouse with integrated haptics, and you can read all about that here.
Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both devices will also be sold to commercial customers, and the Surface Pro 12-inch will be available in an optional 5G configuration.

title_fa: Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button
excerpt_en: Microsoft is launching a second generation of its Surface Mouse next month that includes haptic feedback support. The Surface Mouse also has a customizable action button for the first time, which is primarily designed for quick access to Copilot (of course), but can be...
excerpt_fa: Microsoft is launching a second generation of its Surface Mouse next month that includes haptic feedback support. The Surface Mouse also has a customizable action button for the first time, which is primarily designed for quick access to Copilot (of course), but can be...
content_en:
Microsoft is launching a second generation of its Surface Mouse next month that includes haptic feedback support. The Surface Mouse also has a customizable action button for the first time, which is primarily designed for quick access to Copilot (of course), but can be configured to work with other shortcuts from the Surface app.
Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button
The $79.99 Surface Mouse will start shipping on October 13th.
The $79.99 Surface Mouse will start shipping on October 13th.
“Its haptic feedback adds a small, purposeful physical response to the moment you usually only see on a screen: a click registering, a window snapping into place or an object aligning just right,” says Brett Ostrum, corporate vice president of Surface Devices. “It is subtle by design, but noticeable within seconds — and hard to give up once you have it.”
The haptic feedback works with things like clicks, drags, and alignment throughout Windows 11, but the tactile feedback also triggers in apps like PowerPoint, Affinity, Concepts, and Filmora. Microsoft added support for haptic feedback in Windows 11 earlier this year, and so far it’s mainly Microsoft and Logitech that are supporting it with dedicated hardware. Logitech’s MX Master 4 has haptic feedback, and its Pro X2 Superstrike (and today’s new X3) includes a haptic-based clicks system that doesn’t support the Windows 11 haptic feedback. The upcoming Surface Laptop Ultra also has a haptic trackpad.
After originally launching the Surface Mouse in 2016 and not updating it since, Microsoft has now redesigned it to be more comfortable for all-day use, with a soft-touch material at the top. Thanks to Bluetooth 6.0 support, you can now also pair it with up to three devices.
The new Surface Mouse will be available on October 13th, the same day Microsoft launches its refreshed Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices. It will be priced at $79.99, and available in black and platinum color options.

title_en: Microsoft's new Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 feature Snapdragon X2 Plus chips
title_fa: Microsoft's new Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 feature Snapdragon X2 Plus chips
excerpt_en: Microsoft's smaller Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 are getting a much-needed chip upgrade.
excerpt_fa: Microsoft's smaller Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 are getting a much-needed chip upgrade.
content_en:
Microsoft's new Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 feature Snapdragon X2 Plus chips
There's also a new haptic Surface Mouse on the way.
Microsoft's hardware business seems to be in disarray on all fronts, especially Xbox, but it's still trucking along with refreshed versions of its smaller Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13. The big change is the new Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, which aims to be a solid update from the slower Qualcomm chips powering those devices last year. As Microsoft's smallest PCs, the key for both the Surface Pro 12 and Laptop 13 is portability over raw power. These were also ostensibly low-cost devices last year, with launch prices below $1,000, but as with everything else, the RAMaggedon has bumped the Surface Pro 12-inch up to $1,150 and the Surface Laptop 13 to $1,199.
Design-wise, nothing has changed with either device. The Surface Pro 12-inch is still a small 12-inch tablet with a kickstand, and it can transform into a pseudo-laptop with the $150 Surface Pro keyboard (sold separately, as always, because Microsoft seems to hate smart consumer choices). The Surface Laptop 13, meanwhile, is the company's basic notebook design shrunk down to a 13-inch screen and 2.7-pound frame. Both systems also feature new 500-nit displays, which are 25 percent brighter than before.
I thought the 12-inch tablet was absolutely adorable when I reviewed it last year, and I'm hoping the new internals alleviate my performance concerns. Microsoft claims the Snapdragon X2 Plus chips deliver 60 percent better graphics than the last generation, as well as 95 percent faster on-device AI and 18 percent better battery efficiency. As for basic Office productivity work, the company says the new chip is 18 percent faster. The upgrades sound compelling for anyone who was interested in these smaller Surface devices, but couldn't stomach the major speed downgrade of the previous Snapdragon X chips. If you picked up one of these systems last year, though, it's probably worth waiting a bit longer to upgrade. And if you need more power, the larger 13-inch Surface Pro and Surface Laptop 13.8-inch are also available with newer Snapdragon X2 chips (and much higher pricing of their own).
The Surface Pro 12-inch is also launching together with Microsoft Ink Canvas, an "AI-powered, pen-first experience for sketching, annotating, generating images and summarizing text directly on the canvas," as the company describes. That doesn't sound particularly unique, but at least it's something to do with the Surface Slim Pen. The app will also be available on the Microsoft Store on October 13th for other Surface devices.
Alongside the PC hardware, Microsoft is launching a new $80 Surface Mouse, an ambidextrous mouse with haptic functionality. The company says you'll be able to feel certain Windows 11 interactions, like snapping a window or aligning objects. That's similar to what we've seen with the Logitech MX Master 4. It's an evolution of the previous Surface Mouse, which was notable for evoking Microsoft's classic Intellimouse design.
All of Microsoft's new Surface hardware will be available on October 13.

title_en: Enveda secures $311M to bring more nature-derived AI drugs into clinical trials
title_fa: Enveda secures $311M to bring more nature-derived AI drugs into clinical trials
excerpt_en: The round valued the AI biotech at $2 billion. It is currently testing drugs that treat skin conditions and preserve weight loss after stopping GLP-1s.
excerpt_fa: The round valued the AI biotech at $2 billion. It is currently testing drugs that treat skin conditions and preserve weight loss after stopping GLP-1s.
content_en:
Enveda, a biotech startup that uses AI to discover new drugs in the natural world, has raised a $311 million Series E at a $2 billion valuation. The fresh funding, which was led by Catalio Capital Management, with participation from Iconiq and others, doubles the valuation Enveda achieved 12 months ago.
The idea behind Enveda is that powerful medicines could be harnessed from plants and microbes, rather than synthesized from scratch in a lab. Viswa Colluru, an early employee of Recursion Pharmaceuticals, founded Enveda in 2019 to speed up the process of discovering these new drugs using AI and other techniques.
While AI hasn’t yet produced any FDA-approved drugs, Enveda is among the wave of companies advancing AI-discovered candidates into human clinical trials. The startup is currently testing several drugs in patients, including one targeting severe skin conditions and another designed to help maintain weight loss after stopping GLP-1s.

title_en: Modal Motors is trying to cut China out of electric motors entirely
title_fa: Modal Motors is trying to cut China out of electric motors entirely
excerpt_en: The startup is working on small, light motors with no rare-earth magnets that are suited for drones, fans, and robots.
excerpt_fa: The startup is working on small, light motors with no rare-earth magnets that are suited for drones, fans, and robots.
content_en:
Lately, it seems like everyone is talking about bringing manufacturing back to the United States, especially when it comes to hard tech like drones and robotics. Michael Van Steenburg thinks he’s ahead of the game.
Van Steenburg spent the last decade building all kinds of electric motors in the U.S. and North America, and now he wants to do it again with his new startup, Modal Motors. This time, he wants to ditch rare-earth magnets entirely, in a bid to further separate the U.S. from China’s supply chain.
As one of the founders in Startup Battlefield 200 who will compete at TechCrunch Disrupt next month, he thinks it’s an urgent pitch to make.
“China’s already flexed its muscles a couple times,” Van Steenburg said, referring to the country restricting access to rare-earth products.
There are other companies working on setting up electric motor manufacturing and supply chains in the U.S., but Van Steenburg argues they’re doing it the wrong way by continuing to rely on rare-earth magnets. Domestic supply of those materials is still years away, he said.
“Other people are ‘reshoring,’ [but] they’re basically knocking off Chinese motors and just doing it in the U.S. But they’re hoping that the U.S. rare-earth magnet system is going to get up to speed fast enough,” he said. “It’s going to still be a while longer before they can actually replace China.”
Modal Motors has two products that it’s developing ahead of Disrupt. One is a small electric motor meant for drones that can also work in fans, blowers, and even actuators. It’s designed to “minimize mass while delivering maximum torque density and efficiency,” according to the startup’s website.
The more radical design is what Modal refers to as the “Hybrid Enigma Drive,” a planar — or flat — electric motor that can fit in lower-profile spaces.
Van Steenburg is drawing on decades of experience in the automotive industry to develop these motors and get them customer-ready. But there’s also an irony in the work Van Steenburg is doing to make Modal Motors’ products a China-free option; in the late 1990s, he worked on a hybrid gas-electric drivetrain that China wanted to put in its so-called “People’s Car.”
“It’s kind of comical,” he said, thinking back on that experience and how much the world has changed. What hasn’t changed, he said, is his outsider streak and strong conviction about doing things that are hard.

title_en: Disney+ and Hulu add to the growing trend of streaming inflation
title_fa: Disney+ and Hulu add to the growing trend of streaming inflation
excerpt_en: At the same time, Disney appears to be exploring new ways to expand its streaming business beyond simply raising subscription prices.
excerpt_fa: At the same time, Disney appears to be exploring new ways to expand its streaming business beyond simply raising subscription prices.
content_en:
Streaming is getting more expensive again. Disney is the latest media giant to raise prices for its streaming services, adding to a growing pattern across the industry. The increases come roughly a year after Disney’s last major streaming price hike.
Disney is raising the price of its ad-free Disney+ and Hulu bundle to $21.99 a month, up from $19.99, whereas the ad-free stand-alone plans are each rising to $21.49 per month, up from $18.99. The company is also increasing the price of its stand-alone ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu plans to $12.49 a month.
The new prices are reflected on Disney+’s support page. Bloomberg was the first to report the changes.
Disney+ and Hulu are hardly alone. Streaming companies have spent the past several years steadily increasing prices. Peacock and Apple TV also raised prices in August, while Netflix increased prices earlier this year.
When Disney+ launched in 2019, its basic monthly subscription cost $6.99. Since then, the service has gradually moved further away from that intro price as Disney has tried to turn streaming into a profitable part of its entertainment business.
The latest increases come as streaming remains an increasingly important part of Disney’s overall business. In its third-quarter 2026 results, Disney said entertainment streaming revenue from Disney+ and Hulu rose 11% to $5.5 billion, driven by subscriber growth and the impact of previous price increases.
At the same time, Disney appears to be exploring new ways to expand its streaming business beyond simply raising subscription prices.
The company has reportedly explored the possibility of introducing a free tier for Disney+. This could put the company in more direct competition with platforms such as YouTube and Tubi, which have been capturing a growing share of consumers’ viewing time.
Earlier this month, Disney+ also introduced “Playlists,” a new feature designed to help users discover and continuously watch curated selections of content.
The company is making changes on the technology side as well. Disney recently hired Karandeep Anand as its first-ever chief technology officer. Anand is the former CEO of Character.AI, a company Disney previously accused of infringing on its intellectual property.

title_en: The old cybersecurity model is breaking
title_fa: The old cybersecurity model is breaking
excerpt_en: As concern over AI safety and rogue agents continue to make headlines, it’s no surprise that cybersecurity stocks are rising, or that investors are pouring massive amounts of capital into startups trying to build the next generation of security for an AI-native world. We’re even...
excerpt_fa: As concern over AI safety and rogue agents continue to make headlines, it’s no surprise that cybersecurity stocks are rising, or that investors are pouring massive amounts of capital into startups trying to build the next generation of security for an AI-native world. We’re even...
content_en:
As concern over AI safety and rogue agents continue to make headlines, it’s no surprise that cybersecurity stocks are rising, or that investors are pouring massive amounts of capital into startups trying to build the next generation of security for an AI-native world. We’re even seeing companies like Instinct and Simile bring in nine-figure checks and valuations that wouldn’t have made sense a few years ago.
With a front row seat to it all is Shardul Shah, a partner at Index Ventures who’s spent nearly two decades investing in cybersecurity and enterprise software — including six consecutive rounds in cloud security startup Wiz, which Google acquired for $32 billion earlier this year in one of its largest acquisitions ever.
On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Shah joins Rebecca Bellan to break down why he thinks periodic, human-in-the-loop security can’t keep up anymore, and why Index continues investing in AI-native security companies at stages that once required much more proof.
Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify and all the casts. You also can follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

title_en: Disney+ and Hulu are getting even more expensive (again)
title_fa: Disney+ and Hulu are getting even more expensive (again)
excerpt_en: So I guess we're just doing this every year now.
excerpt_fa: So I guess we're just doing this every year now.
content_en:
Disney+ and Hulu are getting even more expensive (again)
This is the fourth price increase in as many years.
Streamflation strikes again. Disney is raising prices on many of its streaming subscriptions, according to a report by Bloomberg. Disney+ is shooting up to $21.50 per month for the ad-free version, which is a 13 percent increase. The ad-free bundle that includes both Disney+ and Hulu is going up by $2 to $22 per month. That's still a fairly decent deal, as it's around half of what it would cost to purchase each separately.
Ad-supported plans are also getting hit with the price increase hammer. Disney+ with ads is going up to $12.50 a month, from $12, and the same goes for Hulu with ads. However, an ad-supported bundle with both services remains unchanged at $13 per month.
These new prices go into effect today and new customers will see it reflected in their next bill. Engadget has reached out to Disney to ask for more information on the hike and will update this post when we learn more.
This is the fourth price increase for Disney+ and its various bundles in four years. I guess it's just a yearly thing now that we have to accept. It's weird to me that Disney+ keeps going up in price, while the streamer itself keeps cutting content.
It just cancelled Daredevil: Born Again, so the third season in 2027 will be its last. As a matter of fact, that's the final live-action Marvel show that we know of. The company has yet to announce anything else, though VisionQuest is coming later this year. It's also dead on the live-action Star Wars front. The second season of Ahsoka is coming in January, but that's it beyond cartoons. I have no idea what's going on over there. I'm not sure why anyone would pay $21.50 a month for another adaptation of Percy Jackson and the Olympians, but maybe that's just me.
Luckily, the bundles exist. Disney+ seems to be winding down its most popular IPs in favor of theatrical releases, but Hulu is a consistent source of fresh programming. There are plenty of original shows, like Alien: Earth and Paradise, and the platform offers next-day access to content from ABC, Fox and other network channels.

title_en: Zoox grounds Atlanta test fleet after workers report toxic gas exposure symptoms
title_fa: Zoox grounds Atlanta test fleet after workers report toxic gas exposure symptoms
excerpt_en: The repeated incidents led one worker to file a complaint with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, which opened an inquiry and told Zoox to investigate the exposures.
excerpt_fa: The repeated incidents led one worker to file a complaint with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, which opened an inquiry and told Zoox to investigate the exposures.
content_en:
Zoox has grounded its autonomous vehicle test fleet in Atlanta after safety drivers were potentially exposed to carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, or hydrogen sulfide gas inside its vehicles last month, TechCrunch has learned. The repeated incidents led one worker to file a complaint with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, which opened an inquiry and told Zoox to investigate the exposures.
As many as 40 workers were possibly exposed to the gases in the vehicles, according to a letter from OSHA to Zoox that TechCrunch viewed, though the Amazon-owned company says the number is lower.
Zoox put at least one group of workers back on the road in a different car after one vomited and the rest reported exposure symptoms, a contractor told TechCrunch. That second car may have also contained potentially toxic gases, he said, because the workers experienced another bout of exposure symptoms later that day.
“They made us go right back in the field after we said we were throwing up,” Jay Davis, one of the contractors who got sick in mid-August, told TechCrunch in an interview. “I emailed HR, told her what’s going on, and I told her I feel like it’s messed up that y’all made us go [back out].”
Workers reported exposure symptoms and strange smells through much of last month until August 22, when someone called 911 for a sick worker. The facility in northwest Atlanta has operated at limited capacity since then, with the test vehicles quarantined while Zoox investigated the exposures, according to two employees. Zoox’s purpose-built robotaxis, which are all electric, are not affected.
TechCrunch spoke to Davis, who filed the OSHA complaint, along with one current and two former employees for this story. The other three workers were granted anonymity to discuss private company matters and because they fear retaliation.
The illnesses come as Zoox branches into new cities and expands its existing operations in places like Las Vegas and San Francisco, in a bid to catch market leader Waymo. This rapid growth has put some safety monitors at risk. As TechCrunch previously reported, contractors have sustained injuries from sudden braking and swerving in the Zoox test vehicles. Waymo has also reported similar test driver injuries to OSHA.
Exactly what gases the Zoox employees were exposed to remains unclear. Davis said he and two other workers who became sick were told at the emergency room that their symptoms were consistent with carbon monoxide exposure. The complaint filed with OSHA mentions possible carbon dioxide, or CO2, exposure.
Zoox told OSHA in a September 10 letter, viewed by TechCrunch, that it examined its test vehicles for signs of CO2 and replaced their 12-volt batteries. Damaged batteries can produce hydrogen sulfide gas, which creates a “rotten egg” smell. Some of the employees who spoke to TechCrunch said they noticed a similar smell in the cars. (After this story was published, Zoox told TechCrunch it has detected no damage to the batteries and no signs of hydrogen sulfide gas.)
Zoox identified 28 employees who rode in six test vehicles that had an “unexplained odor,” the company said in its letter to OSHA. Zoox told OSHA that 10 workers “voluntarily underwent medical evaluation” to “determine whether any exposure had occurred.” Zoox said in the letter that it received only “one medical report identifying CO2 exposure.”
Zoox told TechCrunch it hasn’t identified the presence of carbon monoxide, which is odorless, in its vehicles. The company said it consulted an outside medical expert to help investigate the issues and that the only gas it detected in the impacted vehicles was CO2.
In the letter to OSHA, the company said it will add CO2 monitors to the vehicles, and Zoox told TechCrunch that these devices will be able to detect other gases like carbon monoxide and hydrogen sulfide. OSHA has since closed its inquiry.
“The safety and well-being of our Zoox test fleet operators is our primary concern in this situation,” the company told TechCrunch. “We are taking ongoing, appropriate, and cautious actions to investigate the reported events as necessary and support any needs from our operators. While we investigate these reports thoroughly, we have ceased operations of our test vehicles in this market.”
Known risks
Cars produce carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide when they burn fuel. These gases can enter a vehicle if there is a leak in the exhaust system; they can also build up if a vehicle runs inside an enclosed space for an extended period. It’s a common enough problem that the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration investigated Ford for six years over reports of carbon monoxide buildup in its Explorer SUVs.
In its letter to OSHA, Zoox said it tested the vehicles’ exhaust systems for leaks and performed a “smoke test” for cabin intrusions. It did not say whether it found any evidence of either. The company also removed all the 12-volt batteries, inspected them for damage, and replaced them. It did not tell OSHA whether it found evidence of damage to the batteries.
The company keeps its test vehicles running through much of a given day, in part to maintain sensor calibration and reduce the onboard self-driving computer’s boot time. Zoox uses an exhaust-capture system at its indoor depots — similar to what is used to capture truck fumes at firehouses — designed to mitigate the buildup of toxic gases.
Zoox modifies the Highlander SUVs it uses for its test fleet. Most of that work focuses on adding sensors and an autonomy computer. But the company makes other changes, too, including adding an interior “snorkel” above the central infotainment screen that pushes air toward rear-seat passengers, the employees told TechCrunch.
Zoox said it doesn’t modify the ventilation systems in these SUVs. But making any changes to a vehicle can increase the risk that gases will leak into the cabin. In the Ford investigation, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said in 2023 that...

title_en: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features
title_fa: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features
excerpt_en: Pro and Plus users will be able to use the Work tab on their phones to complete agentic tasks.
excerpt_fa: Pro and Plus users will be able to use the Work tab on their phones to complete agentic tasks.
content_en:
OpenAI announced on Wednesday that it is bringing voice-based agentic features to mobile, allowing users to trigger workflows like drafting documents or summarizing emails.
Plus and Pro users will be able to use the Work tab on their phone to create a document, draft an email, or summarize Slack messages, for instance. These subscribers can do things like build sites, create presentations, use the cloud browser, and also access other areas like finances in ChatGPT. Free and Go users, meanwhile, will get to work with plugins and connected apps.
OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will have richer text output. Plus, users will be able to switch between text and voice easily. They can also start working on a conversation on the go and resume it on desktop.
The feature arrives as an increasing number of users are turning to voice to issue commands to AI assistants for complex tasks.
In July, OpenAI launched its new conversational model GPT-Live, and later the company integrated it with the desktop app to let users use their voice to complete tasks in the Work tab or build apps in the Codex tab. The new rollout brings similar capabilities to the mobile app.
Recently, Anthropic made the handoff between mobile and desktop easier and also merged its Cowork and Chat interface. But OpenAI is still keeping chat and workspaces separate.

title_en: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it
title_fa: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it
excerpt_en: The report suggests that greater exposure will not resolve the unease around the technology, nor reduce public support for AI regulation.
excerpt_fa: The report suggests that greater exposure will not resolve the unease around the technology, nor reduce public support for AI regulation.
content_en:
People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations.
But using AI every day doesn’t necessarily mean people are feeling comfortable with its implications for the world: About 68% of Americans who use AI daily are worried about it, according to a new survey conducted by opinion research firm Gallup, and concern about the tech skews even higher among people who use it less frequently.
Coming at a time of intense debate around the dangers of AI, quick developments around AI safety, the implications of AI going rogue, and accusations of anticompetitive behavior, these findings complicate the notion that adoption can serve as a straightforward measure of public enthusiasm for AI.
Commissioned by Microsoft, the Gallup study currently has results from 37 countries, where researchers polled about 1,000 people in each country between April and July. The project will eventually span 140 countries. Notably, India, a large population of tech users, is not currently part of the reported results, nor are Australia and Malaysia.
The findings appear to put the U.S. at the anxious end of an international chart even as people in other parts of the world expect the technology to improve their lives. According to Gallup, Western countries are most concerned about AI, with the United States leading in anxiety — 74% of Americans reported feelings of worry, and only 36% expect AI to mostly help the country.
Other wealthy Western countries showed a similar mix of relatively frequent use and concern. In Canada, for example, 29% of those surveyed reported using AI daily, and of those, more than half expressed concerns about the impact of the technology. Overall, 64% of Canadians aware of AI said it worried them.
There’s certainly been a growing wave of discontent around AI, with tech companies laying off hundreds of thousands of employees in order to invest in AI, shrinking entry-level openings, life-ending cases of AI psychosis, and dire warnings from AI leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned that the tech will wipe out jobs en masse.
The survey paints a different picture in the rest of the world, however. In Singapore, which had the highest portion of daily users in the study (46%), more than 80% of those aware about AI expect the tech to improve their everyday lives, and 77% think it’ll help the country. In China, where 35% of people report using AI daily, most people expect it to help the country. The story is similar in Israel.
Still, optimism about AI doesn’t necessarily appear to translate to trust in the tech’s accuracy. According to Gallup, people who use AI daily were generally more trusting of its results, especially in high-adoption countries like Singapore, Israel, and China, while less frequent users remain skeptical across the board. In the U.S., only 45% of daily users expressed that level of confidence. Altogether, only 36% (median) of the people surveyed said they trust AI’s results a lot.
Overall, though, Gallup reports that positivity about AI outweighs negative sentiments: In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people mostly reported feeling curious about the tech, with a fewer number saying they felt happy or excited. Only about 32% of those surveyed said they felt worried about AI. Positive emotions seem to be most common in China (90%), Singapore (89%), and Kenya (87%).
It’s not clear how much sentiment in some countries, especially China, might have changed since the survey ended in July, as the pace of AI development has lately burgeoned into a matter of international importance. AI safety is one of the major topics on the table for discussion when U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping meet on Thursday.
Notably, China’s head of the Ministry of State Security, Chen Yixin, wrote in a recent article that AI will have “a systemic impact on the political and security environment,” and could threaten China’s “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”
“One of the clearest findings is that attitudes toward AI are multidimensional. People can be curious about AI, expect it to be beneficial and use it frequently while still being worried about it. Similarly, they can see considerable potential in AI while remaining skeptical about whether the information it provides is accurate,” Pablo Diego-Rosell, senior scientist at Gallup, told TechCrunch.
While the report paints a picture of optimism colored by some concern, it’s nevertheless true that AI worries are increasingly becoming part of public discourse. People who rely on AI for day-to-day tasks may end up supporting tougher rules or resisting its use in hiring, healthcare, education, or government. And there’s certainly an argument to be made that training and serving AI models can harm the climate, and their unregulated use can disrupt cybersecurity, diminish content ownership, upset the creative arts fields, or harm data privacy.
At the end of the day, the report suggests that greater exposure alone will not resolve the unease around the technology. Still, given the amount of money that’s being invested, AI will likely continue proliferating even as disputes rage around where it belongs and what limits should be placed around it.
